title: Lines & Intersection
description: Represent lines and decide whether and where two segments intersect

blocks.text: A very common geometry question is whether two line segments cross, and if so, where. It sounds easy, but the edge cases make a naive approach fragile.
The robust solution builds directly on the orientation test, which lets us answer the question exactly and without dividing by zero.
There are a few common ways to describe a line, and the right one depends on the task.

items: Two points that lie on it, the most flexible form for segments
Slope and intercept, the familiar y equals m x plus c, but it breaks for vertical lines
The general form a x plus b y plus c equals 0, which handles every line including vertical

blocks.text: For segment problems we usually keep the two endpoints and lean on the orientation test, avoiding slopes entirely.
The core idea uses orientation. Two segments cross in the normal case when each segment has its two endpoints on opposite sides of the other segment line.

blocks.caption: Segments cross when each straddles the line through the other

blocks.text: We check this with four orientation tests: the endpoints of segment one against segment two, and the endpoints of segment two against segment one. If both pairs straddle, the segments cross.
Using the orientation function, the general crossing test is short. It returns true when the two segments properly cross.

codes.python:
# orientation(...) returns 1, -1, or 0 as defined in the orientation topic
def segments_intersect(p1, p2, p3, p4):
    d1 = orientation(p3, p4, p1)
    d2 = orientation(p3, p4, p2)
    d3 = orientation(p1, p2, p3)
    d4 = orientation(p1, p2, p4)
    return d1 != d2 and d3 != d4   # each segment straddles the other

blocks.text: The general test misses the situations where an orientation comes out zero, meaning points are collinear or an endpoint just touches the other segment.

blocks.caption: Split into the general case and the collinear case

blocks.text: When any orientation is zero, check whether that point lies within the bounding box of the other segment. If it does, the segments touch. Handling these on top of the general test makes the check fully correct.

Do not forget the boundaries:

Endpoints touching, overlapping collinear segments, and shared corners are all easy to miss. Decide up front whether touching counts as intersecting for your problem.

If you also need the exact point where two lines meet, solve the two line equations together. This can be done cleanly with cross products, which gives the point without a special case for vertical lines.
Be aware that the intersection of integer lines can have fractional coordinates, so you may need to return a rational or floating point result and handle precision carefully.
